entries.4a45ec5ce560af632cd38dcc55b0d3498ca4ecab: <div sID="gen9852" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Job.25" sID="Job.25"/> <div eID="gen9852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9853" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9854" type="x-p"/> Bildad here makes a very short reply to Job's last discourse, as one that began to be tired of the cause. He drops the main question concerning the prosperity of wicked men, as being unable to answer the proofs Job had produced in the foregoing chapter: but, because he thought Job had made too bold with the divine majesty in his appeals to the divine tribunal (<reference osisRef="Job.23.1-Job.23.17">ch. xxiii.</reference>), he in a few words shows the infinite distance there is between God and man, teaching us, I. To think highly and honourably of God, <reference osisRef="Job.25.2-Job.25.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">5</reference>. II. To think meanly of ourselves, <reference osisRef="Job.25.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.25.6">6</reference>. These, however misapplied to Job, are two good lessons for us all to learn.
entries.84d20500b45ba4856d5d9743a13b23fe7bafb765: <div eID="gen9854" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9853" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God Exalted and Man Abased. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9855" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 Dominion and fear <hi type="italic">are</hi> with him, he maketh peace in his high places. <hi type="super">3</hi> Is there any number of his armies? and upon whom doth not his light arise? <hi type="super">4</hi> How then can man be justified with God? or how can he be clean <hi type="italic">that is</hi> born of a woman? <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold even to the moon, and it shineth not; yea, the stars are not pure in his sight. <hi type="super">6</hi> How much less man, <hi type="italic">that is</hi> a worm? and the son of man, <hi type="italic">which is</hi> a worm? <div eID="gen9855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9856" type="x-p"/> Bildad is to be commended here for two things:—1. For speaking no more on the subject about which Job and he differed. Perhaps he began to think Job was in the right, and then it was justice to say no more concerning it, as one that contended for truth, not for victory, and therefore, for the finding of truth, would be content to lose the victory; or, if he still thought himself in the right, yet he knew when he had said enough, and would not wrangle endlessly for the last word. Perhaps indeed one reason why he and the rest of them let fall this debate was because they perceived that Job and they did not differ so much in opinion as they thought: they owned that wicked people might prosper a while, and Job owned they would be destroyed at last; how little then was the difference! If disputants would understand one another better, perhaps they would find themselves nearer one another than they imagined. 2. For speaking so well on the matter about which Job and he were agreed. If we would all get our hearts filled with awful thoughts of God and humble thoughts of ourselves, we should not be so apt as we are to fall out about matters of doubtful disputation, which are trifling or intricate. <div eID="gen9856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9857" type="x-p"/> Two ways Bildad takes here to exalt God and abase man:— <div eID="gen9857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> I. He shows how glorious God is, and thence infers how guilty and impure man is before him, <reference osisRef="Job.25.2-Job.25.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Let us see then, <div eID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> 1. What great things are here said of God, designed to possess Job with a reverence of him, and to check his reflections upon him and upon his dealings with him: (1.) God is the sovereign Lord of all, and <hi type="italic">with him is terrible majesty. Dominion and fear are with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.25.2">v. 2</reference>. He that gave being has an incontestable authority to give laws, and can enforce the laws he gives. He that made all has a right to dispose of all according to his own will, with an absolute sovereignty. Whatever he will do he does, and may do; and none can say unto him, <hi type="italic">What doest thou?</hi> or <hi type="italic">Why doest thou so?</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.35">Dan. iv. 35</reference>. His having dominion (or being <hi type="italic">Dominus</hi>—<hi type="italic">Lord</hi>) bespeaks him both owner and ruler of all the creatures. They are all his, and they are all under his direction and at his disposal. Hence it follows that he is to be feared (that is, reverenced and obeyed), that he is feared by all that know him (the seraphim cover their faces before him), and that, first or last, all will be made to fear him. Men's dominion is often despicable, often despised, but God is always terrible. (2.) The glorious inhabitants of the upper world are all perfectly observant of him and entirely acquiesce in his will: <hi type="italic">He maketh peace in his high places.</hi> He enjoys himself in a perfect tranquillity. The holy angels never quarrel with him, nor with one another, but entirely acquiesce in his will, and unanimously execute it without murmuring or disputing. Thus the will of God is done in heaven; and thus we pray that it may be done by us and others on earth. The sun, moon, and stars, keep their courses, and never clash with one another: nay, even in this lower region, which is often disturbed with storms and tempests, yet when God pleases he commands peace, by <hi type="italic">making the storm a calm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.29">Ps. cvii. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.65.7">lxv. 7</reference>. Observe, The high places are <hi type="italic">his</hi> high places; for <hi type="italic">the heaven, even the heavens, are the Lord's</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">Ps. cxv. 16</reference>) in a peculiar manner. Peace is God's work; where it is made it is he that makes it, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa. lvii. 19</reference>. In heaven there is perfect peace; for there is perfect holiness, and there is God, who is love. (3.) He is a God of irresistible power: <hi type="italic">Is there any number of his armies?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.25.3">v. 3</reference>. The greatness and power of princes are judged of by their armies. God is not only himself almighty, but he has numberless numbers of armies at his beck and disposal,—standing armies that are never disbanded,—regular troops, and well disciplined, that are never to seek, never at a loss, that never mutiny,—veteran troops, that have been long in his service,—victorious troops, that never failed of success nor were ever foiled. All the creatures are his hosts, angels especially. He is Lord of all, Lord of hosts. He has numberless armies, and yet makes peace. He could make war upon us, but is willing to be at peace with us; and even the heavenly hosts were sent to proclaim <hi type="italic">peace on earth</hi> and <hi type="italic">good will towards men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Luke ii. 14</reference>. (4.) His providence extends itself to all: <hi type="italic">Upon whom does not his light arise?</hi> The light of the sun is communicated to all parts of the world, and, take the year round, to all equally. See <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 6</reference>. That is a faint resemblance of the universal cognizance and care God takes of the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Matt. v. 45</reference>. All are under the light of his knowledge and are naked and open before him. All partake of the light of his goodness: it seems especially to be meant of <hi type="italic">that.</hi> He is good to all; the earth is full of his goodness. He is <hi type="italic">Deus optimus—God, the best of beings,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">maximus—the greatest:</hi> he has power to destroy; but his pleasure is to show mercy. All the creatures live upon his bounty. <div eID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9860" type="x-p"/> 2. What low things are here said of man, and very truly and justly (<reference osisRef="Job.25.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">How then can man be justified with God? Or how can he be clean?</hi> Man is not only mean, but vile, not only earthly, but filthy; he cannot be justified, he cannot be clean, (1.) In comparison with God. Man's righteousness and holiness, at the best, are nothing to God's, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Ps. lxxxix. 6</reference>. (2.) In debate with God. He that will quarrel with the word and providence of God must unavoidably go by the worst. God will be justified, and then man will be condemned, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Ps. li. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Rom. iii. 4</reference>. There is no error in God's judgment, and therefore there lies no exception against it, nor appeal from it. (3.) In the sight of God. If God is so great and glorious, how can man, who is guilty and impure, appear before him? Note, [1.] Man, by reason of his actual transgressions, is obnoxious to God's justice and cannot in himself be justified before him: he can neither plead <hi type="italic">Not guilty,</hi> nor plead any merit of his own to balance or extenuate his guilt. The scripture has concluded all under sin. [2.] Man, by reason of his original corruption, as he is born of a woman, is odious to God's holiness, and cannot be clean in his sight. God sees his impurity, and it is certain that by it he is rendered utterly unfit for communion and fellowship with God in grace here and for the vision and fruition of him in glory hereafter. We have need therefore to be born again of water and of the Holy Ghost, and to be bathed again and again in the blood of Christ, that fountain opened. <div eID="gen9860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9861" type="x-p"/> II. He shows how dark and defective even the heavenly bodies are in the sight of God, and in comparison with him, and thence infers how little, and mean, and worthless, man is. 1. The lights of heaven, though beauteous creatures, are before God as clods of earth (<reference osisRef="Job.25.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold even to the moon,</hi> walking in brightness, and the stars, those glorious lamps of heaven, which the heathen were so charmed with the lustre of that they worshipped them—yet, in God's sight, in comparison with him, they shine not, they are not pure; they have no glory, by reason of the glory which excelleth, as a candle, though it burn, yet does not shine when it is set in the clear light of the sun. The glory of God, shining in his providences, eclipses the glory of the brightest creatures, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Isa. xxiv. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">The moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in Mount Sion.</hi> The heavenly bodies are often clouded; we plainly see spots in the moon, and, with the help of glasses, may sometimes discern spots upon the sun too: but God sees spots in them that we do not see. How durst Job then so confidently appeal to God, who would discover that amiss in him which he was not aware of in himself? 2. The children of men, though noble creatures, are before God but as worms of the earth (<reference osisRef="Job.25.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">How much less</hi> does <hi type="italic">man</hi> shine in honour, how much less is he pure in righteousness <hi type="italic">that is a worm, and the son of man,</hi> whoever he be, <hi type="italic">that is a worm!—a vermin</hi> (so some), not only mean and despicable, but noxious and detestable; <hi type="italic">a mite</hi> (so others), the smallest animal, which cannot be discerned with the naked eye, but through a magnifying glass. Such a thing is man. (1.) So mean, and little, and inconsiderable, in comparison with God and with the holy angels: so worthless and despicable, having his original in corruption, and hastening to corruption. What little reason has man to be proud, and what great reason to be humble! (2.) So weak and impotent, and so easily crushed, and therefore a very unequal match for Almighty God. Shall man be such a fool as to contend with his Maker, who can tread him to pieces more easily than we can a worm? (3.) So sordid and filthy. Man is not pure for he is a worm, hatched in putrefaction, and therefore odious to God. Let us therefore wonder at God's condescension in taking such worms as we are into covenant and communion with himself, especially at the condescension of the Son of God, in emptying himself so far as to say, <hi type="italic">I am a worm, and no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.22.6">Ps. xxii. 6</reference>.  <chapter eID="Job.25"/> <div eID="gen9861" type="x-p"/>

entries.28a47fad6c3815a697aec740dbeb7e23dc1c7bbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5000"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <div sID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> THIRD SERIES.<div eID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.25.1-Job.25.6">Job 25:1-6</reference>. Bildad's Reply.</title> <div sID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> He tries to show Job's rashness (<reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference>), by arguments borrowed from Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>, with which compare <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>.<div eID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5000"/>2. Power and terror, that is, terror-inspiring power.<div eID="gen7396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace in his high places--</hi>implying that His power is such on high as to quell all opposition, not merely there, but on earth also. The Holy Ghost here shadowed forth Gospel truths (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7397" type="x-p"/>
entries.2461e916d63aaaf5ed34c3356a8b80d6f285feca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5001"/><div sID="gen7398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5001"/><hi type="bold">3. armies--</hi>angels and stars (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Is 40:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">Jr 33:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Ge 15:5</reference>; "countless," <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">Da 7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen7398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his light--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7399" type="x-p"/>
entries.382d80b953a5623f105a2acfb3a9d697747282f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5002"/><div sID="gen7400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5002"/>4. (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.4">14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.14">15:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7400" type="x-p"/>
entries.115796a498b969aedc888f31449efb1ef18dacbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5003"/><div sID="gen7401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5003"/>5. "Look up even unto the moon" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>). "Stars" here answer to "saints" (angels) there; "the moon" here to "the heavens" there. Even the "stars," the most dazzling object to man's eye, and the angels, of which the stars are emblems (<reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.1">Re 9:1</reference>), are imperfect in His sight. Theirs is the light and purity but of creatures; His of the Creator. <div eID="gen7401" type="x-p"/>
entries.80533594bc9b60d5e7e3d883543aae86910efd64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5004"/><div sID="gen7402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5004"/>6. (Job 4:19-21; 15:<reference osisRef="Job.21.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen7402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worm ... worm--</hi>Two distinct Hebrew words. The first, a worm bred in putridity; alluding to man's corruption. The second a crawling worm; implying that man is weak and grovelling. <chapter eID="Job.25"/>

entries.5ac8ef1a34a1ee5d1eeb049e6bacbd7af352290e: <div eID="gen17087" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17088" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17089" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17089" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17088" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17090" type="x-p"/> Bildad, the Shuhite, in an irregular speech, shows that God's dominion is supreme, his armies innumerable, and his providence extended over all, <reference osisRef="Job.25.1-Job.25.3">Job 25:1-3</reference>; that man cannot be justified before God; that even the heavenly bodies cannot be reputed pure in his sight; much less man, who is naturally weak and sinful, <reference osisRef="Job.25.4-Job.25.6">Job 25:4-6</reference>. <div eID="gen17090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17091" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17092" type="x-p"/> Bildad the Shuhite - This is the last attack on Job; the others felt themselves foiled, though they had not humility enough to acknowledge it, but would not again return to the attack. Bildad has little to say, and that little is very little to the point. He makes a few assertions, particularly in reference to what Job had said in the commencement of the preceding chapter, of his desire to appear before God, and have his case tried by him, as he had the utmost confidence that his innocence should be fully proved. For this Bildad reprehends Job with arguments which had been brought forth often in this controversy, and as repeatedly confuted, <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.15.16">Job 15:14-16</reference>.
entries.8f0e6d65abf782b08b7386423cb6c2190de52530: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17093" type="x-p"/> Dominion and fear are with him - God is an absolute sovereign; his fear is on all the hosts of heaven; and by his sovereignty he establishes and preserves order in the heavens, and among all the inhabitants of the eternal world: how canst thou, therefore, dare to appeal to him, or desire to appear before him?
entries.c8785f6d934f525a59acdafbd95a62e52ce393a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17094" type="x-p"/> Is there any number of his armies? - He has troops innumerable; he can serve himself of all his creatures; every thing may be a means of help or destruction, according to his Divine will. When he purposes to save, none can destroy; and when he is determined to destroy, none can save. It is vain to trust in his creatures against himself. <div eID="gen17094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17095" type="x-p"/> Upon whom doth not his light arise? - That is, his providence rules over all; he is universal Lord; he causes his sun to arise on the evil and the good, and sends his rain on the just and unjust.
entries.de988ae12399e7ab6bdbf51367cb0e235181cfed: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17096" type="x-p"/> How then can man be justified? - Or, ונה umah, With what, shall a man be justified with God? Though this is no conclusion from Bildad's premises, yet the question is of the highest importance to man. Neither Bildad nor any of his fellows could answer it; the doctrine of redemption through the blood of the cross was then known only through types and shadows. We who live in the Gospel dispensation, can readily answer the question, With what shall miserable man (אנוש enosh) be justified with God? - Ans. By bringing forward, by faith, to the throne of the Divine justice, the sacrificial offering of the Lord Jesus Christ; and confiding absolutely in it, as being a full, sufficient, and complete atonement and sacrifice for his sins, and for the salvation of a lost world. How, or with what (ומה umah) shall he be clean that is born of a woman? - Ans. By receiving that grace or heavenly influence communicated by the power and energy of the eternal Spirit applying to the heart the efficacy of that blood which cleanses from all unrighteousness. This, and this only, is the way in which a sinner, when truly penitent, can be justified before God: and in which a believer, convinced of indwelling sin, can be sanctified and cleansed from all unrighteousness. This is the only means of justification and sanctification, without which there can be no glorification. And these two great works, which constitute the whole of salvation, have been procured for a lost world by the incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was delivered for our offenses, and rose again for our justification; to whom be glory and dominion now and for evermore, Amen!
entries.b29916390136ad4fd889fa6d186b71ff349b3821: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17097" type="x-p"/> Behold even to the moon, and it shineth not - It is continually changing its appearance. It never appears twice in its whole revolution with the same face: it is ever waxing or waning; and its face is variegated with opaque spots. Its changeableness can never be compared with the unchangeable nature of God. <div eID="gen17097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17098" type="x-p"/> Yea, the stars are not pure in his sight - Whatever their excellence may be as stars, it is nothing in comparison with him from whom they have derived their being and splendor. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.14-Job.15.16">Job 15:14-16</reference>. The Targum reads: "Behold, the moon is as yet spotted in her eastern part; the sun shines not; and the stars are not pure in his sight." Some think that by stars are meant those angels who kept not their first estate: this may be so, but I cannot see it in the text. It may, however, mean the heavenly host, as it is supposed to do, <reference osisRef="Job.28.7">Job 28:7</reference>; but I still must hesitate on the propriety of such applications. It is probable this speech of Bildad was delivered in the night-season, when clouds interrupted the bright shining of the moon. The third verse seems to refer immediately to the stars, which to the naked eye are innumerable. The sun is not mentioned, because of his absence. This speech of Bildad is both confused and inconclusive. His reasoning is absurd, and he draws false conclusions from his premises. In the third verse, he says, "Is there any number of his armies? and upon whom does not his light arise?" But how absurd is the conclusion which he draws from his questions: - "How then can a man be justified with God, or he be clean who is born of a woman?" This has no relation to the premises; still to us the question is not difficult, and has already been answered in the notes: "A man can be justified with God," through the blood of Christ; and "he can be clean who is born of a woman." through the sanctification of the Spirit.
entries.5f791d20c9eaeb83fc2b8516ebd9188a254aaa9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17099" type="x-p"/> How much less man, that is a worm? - Or as the Targum - "How much more man, who in his life is a reptile; and the son of man, who in his death is a worm." Almost all the versions read, "Truly man is corruption, and the son of man a worm." The original is degradingly expressive: "Even because אנוש enosh, miserable man, is רמה rimmah, a crawling worm; and the son of Adam, who is תולעה toleah, a worm, or rather maggot, from its eating into and dividing certain substances." - Parkhurst. Thus endeth Bildad the Shuhite, who endeavored to speak on a subject which he did not understand; and, having got on bad ground, was soon confounded in his own mind, spoke incoherently, argued inconclusively, and came abruptly and suddenly to an end. Thus, his three friends being confounded, Job was left to pursue his own way; they trouble him no more; and he proceeds in triumph to the end of the thirty-first chapter.  <chapter eID="Job.25"/> <div eID="gen17099" type="x-p"/>

entries.847c436565e734ec2cfae4eebba91767e9fb451b: <reference osisRef="Job.25.1-Job.6.1">Job 25:1-6   1</reference>  Then began Bildad the Shuhite, and said:   2  Dominion and terror are with Him, <div eID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> He maketh peace in His high places.   3  Is there any number to His armies, <div eID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> And whom doth not His light surpass?   4  How could a mortal be just with God, <div eID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> And how could one born of woman be pure?   5  Behold, even the moon, it shineth not brightly, <div eID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> And the stars are not pure in His eyes.   6  How much less mortal man, a worm, <div eID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7973" type="x-p"/> And the son of man, a worm!<hi type="italic">Ultimum hocce classicum, </hi>observes Schultens, <hi type="italic">quod a parte triumvirorum sonuit, magis receptui canentis videtur, quam praelium renovantis.</hi> Bildad only repeats the two commonplaces, that man cannot possibly maintain his supposedly perverted right before God, the all-just and all-controlling One, to whom, even in heaven above, all things cheerfully submit, and that man cannot possibly be accounted spotlessly pure, and consequently exalted above all punishment before Him, the most holy One, before whom even the brightest stars do not appear absolutely pure. המשׁל is an <hi type="italic">inf. abs.</hi> made into a substantive, like השׁקט; the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. (to cause to rule), which is otherwise causative, can also, like <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, signify to rule, or properly, without destroying the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>-signification, to exercise authority (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference>); המשׁל therefore signifies sovereign rule. עשׂה, with הוּא to be supplied, which is not unfrequently omitted both in participial principal clauses (Job 12:17., <reference osisRef="Ps.22.29">Psa 22:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Isa 40:19</reference>, comp. Zec 9:12, where אני is to be supplied) and in partic. subordinate clauses (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">Psa 55:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.10">Hab 2:10</reference>), is an expression of the simple <hi type="italic">praes.,</hi> which is represented by the <hi type="italic">partic</hi>. used thus absolutely (including the personal pronoun) as a proper tense-form (Ew. §168, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, 306, <hi type="italic">d</hi>). Schlottman refers עשׂה to המשׁל ופהד; but the analogy of such attributive descriptions of God is against it. Umbreit and Hahn connect בּמרומיו with the subject: He in His heights, i.e., down from His throne in the heavens. But most expositors rightly take it as descriptive of the place and object of the action expressed: He establishes peace in His heights, i.e., among the celestial beings immediately surrounding Him. This, only assuming the abstract possibility of discord, might mean: <hi type="italic">facit magestate sua ut in summa pace et promptissima obedientia ipsi ministrent angeli ipsius in excelsis</hi> (Schmid). But although from <reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>, nothing more than that even the holy ones above are neither removed from the possibility of sin nor the necessity of a judicial authority which is high above them, can be inferred; yet, on the other hand, from <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.13">Job 9:13</reference> (comp. Job 26:12.), it is clear that the poet, in whose conception, as in scripture generally, the angels and the stars stand in the closest relation, knows of actual, and not merely past, but possibly recurring, instances of hostile dissension and titanic rebellion among the celestial powers; so that עשׂה שׁלום, therefore, is intended not merely of a harmonizing reconciliation among creatures which have been contending one against another, but of an actual restoration of the equilibrium that had been disturbed through self-will, by an act of mediation and the exercise of judicial authority on the part of God.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="25" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. THen answered Bildad <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Not to that which <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> spake last, but to that which stuck most in <ns0:hi>Bildad's</ns0:hi> mind, and which seemed most reprovable in all his discourses; to wit, his bold censure of God's proceedings with him, and his avowed and oft repeated desire of disputing the mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter with him.</ns0:note> the Shuhite, and said,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Dominion <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Absolute and sovereign power over all persons and things, with whom to contend, is both rebellion and madness.</ns0:note> and fear <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Active<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly understood, or <ns0:hi>terrour, i. e.</ns0:hi> that which justly makes him dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />full to all men, and especially to all that shall undertake to dispute with him; awful Majesty, infinite knowledge, whereby he knows men's hearts and ways, far better than they know themselves, and sees much s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>n in them which themselves do not discover, and ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />act purity and justice, which renders him formidable to sinners.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Emphatically spoken<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> with him whom thou challengest, with him who is not lightly and irreverently to be named<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> much less to be contended with. And therefore it is thy duty to humble thy self for thy presumptuous words and carriages towards him, and quietly and modestly to submit thy self and thy cause to his pleasure. This Clause, as well as the following Verse, seems to be added to prove what he last said of God's dominion and dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness: He keepeth and ruleth all persons and things in Heaven in peace and harmony, and the order which he hath established among them. The Angels though they be very numerous and differing in orders and ministeries, do all own his Soveraignty, and acquiesce in his Pleasure, without any disputing and murmuring. The Stars and heavenly Bodies though va<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t in their bulk, and va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious in their motions, yet exactly keep their courses and the order which God hath appointed them: And therefore it is great folly and impudence to exempt thy self from God's jurisdiction, or to quarrel with the methods of God's dealings with thee.</ns0:note>, he ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />keth peace in his high places.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. Is there any number of his armies <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of the Angels, and Stars, and other Creatures, all which are his Hosts wholly submitting themselves to his Will, to be and do what God would have them: And therefore how insolent and unreasonable a thing is it for thee to quarrel with him! He spoke before of God's making peace; and here he mentions the Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies by which he keeps it.</ns0:note>? and upon whom doth not his light arise?<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. properly, his Sun, which riseth upon all, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 45. Or rather 2. metaphorically, all that is in men, which is or may be called <ns0:hi>light,</ns0:hi> the light of life, by which men subsist and are kept out of the state of the dead, called a <ns0:hi>land of darkness,</ns0:hi> Job 10. 22. The Light of Reason and Understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, called God's <ns0:hi>Candle,</ns0:hi> Prov. 20. 27. by which thou, O <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> art capable of arguing with God and with us, and all that peace, and prosperity, and comfort which thou ever didst enjoy, which oft comes under the name of <ns0:hi>Light,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Esth.</ns0:hi> 8. 15, 16. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 97. 11. & 112. 4. which being here called <ns0:hi>light,</ns0:hi> is to continue the Meta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phor, most fitly said to <ns0:hi>arise</ns0:hi> upon men: all this is from God, and therefore is wholly at his disposal, he freely gave it all, and he may justly take it away; as thou thy self didst truly observe and confess, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 21. and consequently thou hast no reason to reproach God for disposing of his own as he pleaseth. Thou hast lost no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing which was thine own, and having no propriety, there is no foundation for any judicial contest with God.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 4. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and 15. 14, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> How then, can man <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The word signifies <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> that is <ns0:hi>miserable,</ns0:hi> which supposeth him to be sinful; and that such a Creature should quarrel with that Dominion of God, to which the sinless, and happy, and glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious Angels willingly submit, is most absurd and impious.</ns0:note> be justified with God <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Before God's Tribunal, to which thou doest so boldly appeal. Thou mayst plead thy Cause with thy fellow-worms as we are, and expect to be justified, but wo to thee if the great God under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />take to plead his Cause against thee; how severely and certainly wouldest thou then be condemned!</ns0:note>? or how can he <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> clean that is born of a woman <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, after the ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary course; for otherwise Christ was born of a Woman, but in a singular manner. This Birth is alledged as an Evidence of man's filthiness, <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> 14. 4. & 15. 14. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 51. 5. and of his liableness to God's Curse and Wrath, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3. 16. <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 2. 2. and consequently of his condemnation opposite to the justification here mentioned, and confidently expected by <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> in this Contest.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:406" />5. Behold even to the moon, and it shineth not <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Moon, though a bright and glorious Creature, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 26. <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 6. 10. if compared with the splendour of the Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine Majesty, is but as a dark and earthy lump, without any lustre or glory. He names the <ns0:hi>Moon</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Stars,</ns0:hi> rather than the <ns0:hi>Sun,</ns0:hi> because they many times are eclipsed or disappear even to our Eyes, which is a plain evidence of their utter obscurity in re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect of God's Light: whereas the Sun, though that also be ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scure, if compared with God, yet it casts a constant and most clear light. Or by naming the <ns0:hi>Moon,</ns0:hi> and thence proceeding to the <ns0:hi>Stars,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Sun</ns0:hi> is included between them.</ns0:note>. yea, the stars are not pure in his sight <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He can discern many spots and blemishes in them which we cannot see; and in like manner he can discover those corruptions or sins in us which are unknown to our own Consciences, which should make thee, O <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> tremble to appear before his Tribunal.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. How much less man <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 22. 6.</ns0:note> worm <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To wit, mean, and vile, and impotent, proceeding from corruption, and returning to it, and withal filthy and loathsom, and so every way a very unfit person to appear before the high and holy God, and much more to contend with him.</ns0:note>: and the son of man <ns0:hi>which is</ns0:hi> a worm <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The same thing repeated in other words; onely for <ns0:hi>miserable man</ns0:hi> in the last Branch he here puts <ns0:hi>the son of</ns0:hi> any <ns0:hi>man,</ns0:hi> of what degree or quality soever, to shew that this is true even of the greatest and best of men.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
